title: On-Call & Incident Response
summary: Being paged at 2am is a role, not a punishment, and it has its own discipline: severity, roles, and communication that turn a solo debugging session into a coordinated response.

slides.markdown:
Everything so far in this group is about how one engineer finds a bug. On-call is about what happens when that bug is live, in production, affecting real users right now, and someone has to be the first person to notice and respond — often alone, often at an inconvenient hour.

What makes on-call its own discipline isn't the debugging itself; it's everything around it: how severity gets decided, who does what when more than one person joins, and how the team communicates while the fire is still burning. Get those wrong and even a correct diagnosis arrives too late or gets lost in confusion.

The core principle that reframes almost everything else here: **mitigate first, understand later.** An outage doesn't wait for a root cause.

slides.subTitle: Being the first responder to production alerts
slides.markdown:
On-call means one engineer (or a small rotation) is designated as the first human to see and act on production alerts outside normal working hours or attention — the person a page goes to when [production-debugging-observability](production-debugging-observability)'s dashboards and alerts fire and nobody's actively watching them.

The job isn't to personally fix every problem end to end. It's to **triage fast**: is this real, how bad is it, does it need to wake up more people, and can I mitigate it myself in the next few minutes? A good on-call engineer escalates appropriately rather than heroically debugging alone for hours while the outage continues — knowing when you're out of your depth is as much the job as knowing how to fix things.

On-call exists because production systems don't fail on a schedule, and the alternative — nobody watching outside business hours — means outages run unbounded until someone happens to notice.

slides.subTitle: How severity drives response urgency
slides.markdown:
Not every alert deserves the same response, and treating them all identically either burns people out (paging hard for a minor blip) or misses real emergencies (a routine-looking alert that's actually critical). **Severity levels** (often Sev-1 through Sev-4, or P0-P3 — naming varies by org) exist to standardize that judgment.

A typical scheme: **Sev-1** — full outage or data loss, all-hands, page immediately, executive visibility. **Sev-2** — significant degradation for many users, urgent but not all-hands. **Sev-3** — limited impact, a subset of users or a non-critical feature, can often wait for business hours. **Sev-4** — cosmetic or negligible, ticket it and move on.

Severity isn't just a label — it determines *everything downstream*: how many people get paged, whether a status page update goes out, whether leadership is notified, and how much process (a full postmortem vs. a quick note) follows afterward. Getting the initial severity call right, fast, is one of the highest-leverage decisions in the first five minutes of an incident.

slides.subTitle: Commander, communicator, responders
slides.markdown:
Once an incident grows past one person, **role separation** prevents the response itself from becoming chaotic:

- **Incident commander** — coordinates the response, makes final calls under uncertainty, decides severity and when to escalate or stand down. Explicitly does *not* need to be the person debugging — their job is coordination, not diagnosis.
- **Communicator** — owns updates to stakeholders, status pages, and internal channels, so responders aren't context-switching between debugging and answering "is this fixed yet" every two minutes.
- **Responders** — the engineers actively investigating and mitigating, reporting findings up to the commander rather than each independently deciding what to tell leadership.

Without this separation, the person best equipped to debug often ends up also fielding Slack messages from six different stakeholders, which is a direct tax on the thing that actually ends the incident. At small scale, one person may hold two roles — but naming the roles explicitly, even briefly, prevents the default failure mode of everyone doing everything and nothing being owned.

An incident's shape is the same almost every time, and naming the stages explicitly helps a team recognize which one it's in: **detect** (an alert fires or a user reports it) → **triage** (assess severity, assemble the right people) → **mitigate** (stop the bleeding — rollback, failover, feature-flag off) → **resolve** (the mitigation holds, impact has actually stopped) → **follow-up** (postmortem, action items, the work covered in the next topic).

The stage most often skipped or rushed is triage — teams jump from detect straight to "someone just start fixing it," which is how you end up with the person best suited to investigate also handling stakeholder questions with no severity call made and no one tracking whether the mitigation actually worked.

slides.markdown:
The single most important reframe for incident response: your job during the incident is to **stop the impact**, not to fully understand it. A rollback that ends customer impact in 3 minutes beats a root-cause fix that takes 45 minutes to develop correctly, even though the rollback teaches you nothing new about *why* it broke.

This inverts the instinct from solo debugging, where [systematic-debugging-method](systematic-debugging-method) rightly insists on understanding root cause before considering something fixed. Under active user impact, that discipline is deferred, not abandoned — you mitigate now (rollback the deploy, fail over to a backup region, flip a feature flag off) and do the careful root-cause investigation from [postmortems-and-incident-learning](postmortems-and-incident-learning) afterward, with the pressure off and the evidence preserved.

The trap to avoid: mitigating in a way that destroys the evidence you'll need later (like restarting every affected process, wiping the very state that would explain what happened) — mitigate with the least destructive action that stops the bleeding.

slides.subTitle: Status pages, stakeholder updates, avoiding silence
slides.markdown:
Silence during an incident is read as either "nothing is happening" or "it's worse than we're saying," neither of which is good — even when the honest update is "we're still investigating, no new information." Regular updates on a fixed cadence (every 15-30 minutes for a serious incident) at minimum confirm the incident is being actively worked, independent of whether there's real news.

A status page update serves a different audience than an internal Slack thread: customers need to know *is this affecting me* and *roughly when will it be resolved*, not the technical detail of which service degraded. Internal stakeholders (support, leadership) need enough detail to answer customer questions and make business decisions, without needing the full technical thread.

The communicator role exists specifically so this doesn't fall on whoever's actively debugging — someone context-switching between a stack trace and a customer-facing status update is both a slower debugger and a worse communicator than either task done by a focused person.

slides.subTitle: Alert fatigue vs missing real incidents
slides.markdown:
| | Too little escalation | Too much escalation |
|---|---|---|
| Symptom | On-call engineer debugs alone for hours on something beyond their expertise | Every minor blip pages someone, often at 3am |
| Consequence | Outage runs longer than necessary; burnout from feeling unsupported | Alert fatigue — real pages get the same shrug as noise, eventually ignored |
| Root cause | No clear policy for when to pull in help, or a culture that discourages asking | Alerting thresholds too sensitive, or no severity-based routing |

Both failure modes come from the same underlying problem: **escalation policy isn't calibrated**. The fix for both is the same discipline — alerts should be tuned to page only for things that need immediate human action, not informational noise, and the on-call engineer should have an explicit, low-friction way to escalate (page the secondary, or start an incident and pull in the service owner) the moment something exceeds their ability to make progress alone, with no stigma attached to using it.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagnosing for an hour while the outage continues
slides.markdown:
The single most common on-call failure mode: an engineer gets paged, starts investigating, gets absorbed in an interesting root-cause hunt, and an hour later the outage is still live because nobody stepped back to ask "what would stop the bleeding right now, even without understanding why."

This usually isn't a knowledge gap — it's a framing gap. Solo debugging habits (don't stop until you understand root cause) are exactly wrong for active incidents, where a rollback you don't fully understand yet is often the correct move, and can be executed in parallel with continued investigation once impact has stopped.

A concrete guard against this: at a fixed time check-in (say, 10-15 minutes in), explicitly ask "do we have a mitigation we could ship right now, even an imperfect one?" — not "do we understand the bug yet." If a deploy correlates with the start time, roll it back before you've finished explaining why it broke; you can explain why afterward, with the customer impact already stopped.

On-call is where every earlier topic in this group gets used under time pressure: reading logs and traces to triage fast, the tools from [debugging-tools-techniques](debugging-tools-techniques) and [production-debugging-observability](production-debugging-observability) to investigate, and the discipline from [concurrency-bugs-and-heisenbugs](concurrency-bugs-and-heisenbugs) if the incident turns out to be a rare timing bug.

But the incident isn't over when impact stops — resolve is stage four of five. The final stage, follow-up, is where a mitigated incident becomes durable organizational learning instead of a scary story that repeats in six months. That's the subject of the next and final topic in this group.
